meta.name: Reverse Engineer Lab
meta.description: An independent catalog of reverse engineering research.

data.title: Digits: source transactions versus the ledger
data.target_version: Connect API v1; public documentation reviewed 2026-10-30
data.question: When an integration successfully writes a financial record, what has actually become true? This investigation separates acceptance of source data from the existence of an accounting result, then follows the identity needed to reconcile the two.
data.summary: How Digits separates imported records from accounting results, and why source identity, replay and ledger visibility are different concerns.
data.observed:
The public Source vs Ledger guide describes two layers: independent source streams retain upstream records, while the ledger presents a merged accounting view. Source writes and ledger reads therefore describe different stages of the contract. The guide also describes eventual visibility between those stages. A successful source request should not be interpreted as a synchronous promise that a corresponding ledger transaction can already be read.

The Identifiers guide makes source identity operational: an external identifier belongs to a source-specific key space. Repeated writes for that identifier refer to one object; sync endpoints use the most recent submitted properties. Digits-provided IDs identify records inside the accounting system. These are different identifiers with different ownership.
data.inferred:
The useful architectural boundary is provenance versus interpretation. Preserving the upstream identity gives a client something stable to replay and investigate, while the accounting layer can combine evidence from multiple origins. It does not follow that every source record produces exactly one ledger transaction.

For example, a payment-processor payout and a bank deposit can describe one economic movement. Matching them is a separate question from deduplicating a retry of the processor record. Treating both situations as the same kind of duplicate would confuse transport reliability with accounting reconciliation.
data.unknown: This is a static analysis of the cited public contract, not a measurement of a connected business account. No money, ledger or live integration was changed. Processing latency, matching heuristics, race behavior and correction propagation were not reproduced. The guides support the two-layer model; they do not establish the internal database, queue technology or a universal one-to-one mapping. Treat those implementation details as unknown.
data.author: Reverse Engineer Lab
data.models: Illustrative identity model: (source, external ID) identifies an imported object; a ledger ID identifies an accounting result. Retain both when building an audit trail. Do not replace the external ID with the ledger ID or assume equal ID strings from two sources name the same object.
data.workflows:
Worked example, not a production trace: an importer reads upstream payout P-104, writes it using the same external identity on retries, and records that source acceptance succeeded. A separate read checks the resulting ledger state. If the ledger result is not yet visible, the importer can report “accepted; accounting result pending” instead of inventing another payout.

A focused verification would replay the same source identity, change an allowed property through the documented sync contract, and observe ledger visibility separately. Record the request outcome and later read outcome as two pieces of evidence. The acceptance criterion is identity stability, not an assumed fixed processing delay.

data.title: Campfire: bank feeds and journal entries
data.question: Does importing a bank transaction mean creating a journal entry? The public API exposes both workflows, so this investigation asks which state each operation represents and where an integration should verify accounting consequences.
data.summary: A contract-level look at bank-feed ingestion, journal construction and the distinction between a recorded bank event and a posted accounting result.
data.observed:
Campfire publishes separate bank-feed and journal-entry workflows. The journal guide begins with retrieving references needed to construct a journal for the intended entity, then supplying its accounting lines. The bank-feed surface represents incoming banking information. The documented bank-sync option to skip journal creation means ingestion and posting are not interchangeable concepts.

These interfaces give an operator two distinct things to inspect: the imported event and the journal that expresses an accounting decision. The presence of one does not, by itself, prove that the other exists or contains the intended accounts and amounts.
data.inferred:
A useful interpretation is that ingestion answers “what did the external feed report?” while a journal answers “how is this event represented in the accounts?” Keeping those questions separate makes duplicate diagnosis clearer. A retry of an import and a second accounting entry are different failure modes.

The separation also changes status language. “Imported” is a defensible statement about a feed record. “Posted” needs evidence from the accounting object. Reporting every accepted feed item as posted would hide the very distinction the API allows.
data.unknown: No live feed was connected and no journal was posted for this article. The analysis does not establish how every tenant configures automatic posting, matching or closed-period controls. It also does not prove transaction isolation, event ordering or webhook delivery guarantees. Consult the endpoint contract and observe the resulting records before treating a transport response as final accounting state.
data.author: Reverse Engineer Lab
data.models: Conceptual model: bank account → incoming bank event → review or matching decision → journal and accounting lines. This is a client-facing reasoning model, not a claim that Campfire implements these stages as four independent services. Entity and account references are part of the journal context and should remain visible in integration records.
data.workflows:
Illustrative scenario: a bank feed reports a 100-unit deposit. A client using the documented skip-journal mode should verify the imported event separately from any later accounting entry. A reviewer may then associate it with an existing transaction or create an appropriate journal. The example amount describes a test case, not an accounting recommendation.

A bounded test plan would record the selected feed mode, inspect the resulting banking record, then look for a journal using the documented relationship or reference. A second test would deliberately use the explicit journal workflow and verify entity, line references and returned status. Those observations establish behavior more reliably than counting successful HTTP requests.

data.title: DOSS: workflows over shared operational data
data.question: What makes an operational workflow more than a sequence of API calls? DOSS’s public descriptions put shared records alongside event- and schedule-driven automation. This investigation examines the implications without presenting marketing descriptions as proof of internal implementation.
data.summary: What DOSS’s public workflow and master-data surfaces reveal about triggers, shared records and the boundary between automation and business state.
data.observed:
DOSS describes workflows that connect operational records and decisions, including purchase approvals, order routing and document matching. Its master-data surface names shared business entities such as products, suppliers and bills of materials. These descriptions emphasize work performed over common data rather than unrelated copies in each module.

The cited pages are public product documentation. They establish the advertised model and examples; they do not provide a public execution trace proving scheduling, persistence or isolation behavior. That evidence distinction matters when reasoning about configurable enterprise software.
data.inferred:
If two workflows read the same supplier or product, a change to that record can alter both workflows’ outcomes. The important design question becomes dependency management: which automations depend on a field, what value do they observe, and who can change it? This follows from shared data; it does not prove a particular dependency engine.

Similarly, “approval” should be treated as business state with an authorized transition, not merely a notification. A useful model separates the trigger, the record under review, the decision and any subsequent external action. Replaying a trigger should not silently manufacture a new business decision.
data.unknown: No authenticated DOSS workspace or proprietary client bundle is published here. Workflow retries, concurrency, audit history, schema-change handling and permission enforcement were not reproduced. The conceptual diagram is an analytical model of the public offering, not verified backend topology. An implementation evaluation should request direct evidence for these operational guarantees rather than infer them from a feature name.
data.author: Reverse Engineer Lab
data.models: Conceptual sequence: shared record → trigger → conditions and decision → recorded outcome. A supplier belongs to master data; a purchase order refers to that supplier; an approval is an outcome on the order. Keeping those identities distinct helps explain what an automation changed and why.
data.workflows:
Illustrative example: a purchase order references a supplier and a requested amount. A workflow starts when the order reaches a review state, checks the relevant business conditions, and records an approval or rejection before the next step. If supplier data changes during review, an operator needs to know whether the workflow uses a snapshot or current values. The public material does not settle that question.

A useful demonstration would inspect one order before and after its trigger, record the rule inputs, repeat the same trigger, and inspect the decision history. Then change one referenced field in a controlled test and observe whether an in-flight workflow changes. These tests distinguish actual behavior from what a workflow diagram suggests.

data.title: Katana: on-hand, committed and expected stock
data.question: Why can a single “stock” number mislead an inventory integration? Katana exposes quantities for physical holdings, commitments and expected supply. This investigation follows the different questions those fields answer at a specific variant and location.
data.summary: Why Katana’s inventory contract needs several quantities, with a worked planning example and explicit limits on what those numbers prove.
data.observed:
The inventory reference identifies an inventory point by variant_id and location_id. It distinguishes quantity_in_stock, quantity_committed and quantity_expected, rather than collapsing physical holdings and future obligations into one field. The same object includes a safety-stock threshold and separate valuation fields.

Sales-order rows and manufacturing relationships add context to demand, while purchasing and production can contribute future supply. A stock reading therefore needs both its identity and its quantity type. A number without a location, variant and meaning is an incomplete observation.
data.inferred:
On-hand stock answers a physical-balance question. Commitments describe demand already associated with that stock; expected supply describes a future event. Adding expected units to on-hand units may help planning, but it does not prove those units can be picked today. Likewise, subtracting commitments is a model of availability, not proof of the order in which reservations will win.

This distinction is especially useful when a storefront, warehouse and purchasing screen display different numbers. They may be answering different questions correctly. The first diagnostic step is to compare definitions and scope before treating a mismatch as stale synchronization.
data.unknown: No warehouse, order or stock movement was changed for this article. Reservation priority, concurrent allocations, partial receipts, costing adjustments and negative-stock behavior were not reproduced. The public object reference supports the quantity distinction but does not establish serializable allocation or a delivery promise. The diagram is a conceptual view of the contract, not Katana’s internal service architecture.
data.author: Reverse Engineer Lab
data.models: Illustrative snapshot: on hand 20 units, committed 8, expected 10. A simple present-stock-minus-demand view gives 12 units; a future planning view gives 22 before any safety-stock allowance. These are worked calculations for understanding the fields, not claims that every Katana availability screen uses those exact formulas. The 10 expected units are not physically present.
data.workflows:
A bounded verification can read one variant/location, inspect an order that contributes demand, and inspect the document behind expected replenishment. After a controlled receipt or fulfillment, compare the same fields again. Keep timestamps and document states so a changed balance can be explained.

For integrations, name each exported quantity explicitly: “on hand” and “expected” are safer than an ambiguous “stock” field. If only one number can be sent downstream, document the chosen interpretation and what it excludes. This prevents an accidental promise of future inventory as immediately shippable inventory.

data.title: Shiptheory: shipment data and service selection
data.question: What should a shipping integration consider complete: sending shipment data, selecting a service, receiving a label or handing a parcel to a carrier? Shiptheory’s public interface exposes several of these concerns, which should remain distinct in a client’s state model.
data.summary: Separate the shipment you describe, the service selected by rules, and the carrier result before treating a label request as fulfillment.
data.observed:
Shiptheory’s developer documentation covers shipment creation and lookup, labels, available delivery services and package sizes. Shipping rules provide a separate selection layer over the shipment description. Addresses, parcels and item information describe what is being shipped; a carrier service describes how it is intended to move.

A label is an artifact associated with a booking outcome. It is not physical proof that the parcel was packed, collected or delivered. Those later events need their own evidence. The API surface is useful precisely because a client can inspect more than one stage instead of representing everything as a single “shipped” flag.
data.inferred:
Model the request and its outcome separately. An accepted shipment description can still encounter a service constraint, a carrier validation problem or a later operational failure. Changing a rule may change a future service decision without changing the order’s commercial identity.

This suggests keeping stable shipment identity, selected service and returned carrier artifacts as separate fields. A retry should be reconciled against the existing shipment before creating a fresh booking, especially if the first response was lost. This is a recommended client discipline, not a claim of undocumented idempotency guarantees.
data.unknown: This article does not establish carrier-specific eligibility, label charging, cancellation or refund semantics. It does not equate a label with carrier collection or delivery. Exact retry guarantees and asynchronous result timing must come from the relevant documented operation and direct testing. No customer address, commercial shipment, carrier credentials or private fulfillment data is included.
data.author: Reverse Engineer Lab
data.models: Conceptual sequence: shipment description → rule/service selection → carrier booking result → label and tracking evidence. An order can require more than one parcel or shipment, so an order identifier alone need not identify a unique carrier artifact. A client should preserve the reference that distinguishes the individual shipment.
data.workflows:
Illustrative scenario: one order is split into two physical shipments. Each shipment needs its own reference and booking result even if both display the same customer order number. If the network times out after the first request, the safe diagnostic question is whether that shipment already exists—not whether the order has any tracking number.

A controlled verification would inspect available services, submit a test shipment through an authorized test route, retrieve the resulting record and compare its selected service and label state. A second test would use an intentionally ineligible service condition and observe the returned failure. No such live booking was performed for this publication.

data.title: Shopify GraphQL: query cost and cursor pagination
data.target_version: Admin GraphQL API 2026-10; public documentation reviewed 2026-10-30
data.question: Why can two successful GraphQL requests consume different capacity, and why is a page number not enough to resume a read? Shopify’s Admin GraphQL contract separates query cost from connection traversal. A reliable reader needs to track both.
data.summary: A worked client model for Shopify’s query-cost budget and cursor pagination, showing why page position and request capacity are separate concerns.
data.observed:
Shopify documents cost-based limits for Admin GraphQL and distinguishes requested cost from actual cost. Query shape and selected fields matter; a request is not simply one interchangeable unit of capacity. The response can expose cost and throttle information that a client uses to plan subsequent work.

Connections use cursor pagination. A reader requests a bounded set of results and uses pageInfo, including the continuation cursor and whether another page exists, to advance. The cursor is supplied by the API. It is not a numeric offset the client should invent or interpret as an internal row identifier.
data.inferred:
The client has two independent state variables: where to continue and when capacity permits another request. Increasing a page size may reduce request count while increasing the cost of each request. Selecting more nested fields may also change cost. Optimizing only for fewer HTTP calls can therefore be counterproductive.

A saved cursor is a continuation token for a particular traversal. It should travel with the relevant query, filters and API version. Reusing it after changing the query shape without checking the contract would combine two different read plans.
data.unknown: The analysis targets the cited Admin GraphQL baseline and public usage guides. It does not promise that a long traversal is a frozen snapshot while records change. Store plan limits, authorization scopes and field costs must be checked for the actual query and API version. No shop data, token, mutation or live rate-limit experiment was used.
data.author: Reverse Engineer Lab
data.models: Illustrative cost calculation, not a published plan limit: if a response reports 120 currently available points and a proposed query requests 80, the client has enough reported capacity at that instant. If a later response reports only 30, blindly sending the same query is a different decision. A reader should use returned throttle information rather than a fixed sleep copied from another shop.
data.workflows:
A useful loop is: request one page; inspect data and GraphQL errors; record cost information; process the returned nodes; save the continuation cursor; then advance only when hasNextPage indicates more data. If the process stops after persisting the cursor but before persisting the page’s work, the next run may skip work. Checkpoint design is therefore part of correctness, separate from pagination syntax.

A bounded verification would compare a small field selection with a wider one, inspect their reported costs, and traverse a known multi-page result while recording returned cursors. This is a proposed validation method, not a claim that this article ran against a shop.
data.apis: The documented GraphQL read surface uses query selections and connections. Throttle metadata describes available query capacity; pageInfo describes position within a connection.

data.title: Klaviyo: API revisions and rate-limit windows
data.question: What makes a Klaviyo request reproducible over time? The URL alone is insufficient when an API revision selects behavior and endpoint-specific windows control throughput. This investigation treats version selection and request scheduling as parts of the contract.
data.summary: How explicit API revisions and separate burst/steady limits affect a Klaviyo client’s retry, scheduling and compatibility decisions.
data.observed:
Klaviyo publishes dated API revisions and endpoint-specific rate limits. Its rate-limit guide describes separate burst and steady windows, measured over one second and one minute, and HTTP 429 when a limit is reached. New API endpoints are documented as account-scoped for this limiting behavior.

The public changelog gives version changes a visible history. A client that records its chosen revision can associate behavior with a particular contract instead of attributing every difference to the same timeless API. That is different from merely storing the SDK package version.
data.inferred:
A request can fit a minute’s average budget and still exceed a short burst window. Conversely, spreading a burst does not guarantee that sustained traffic fits the longer window. Separate jobs that share an account can consume the same capacity even if each job appears modest in isolation.

Retries also need classification. A temporary capacity response and an invalid request body are not the same problem. Retrying an unchanged invalid body faster will not repair it. A client should retain enough response context to distinguish throttling, validation, authentication and server failures without logging credentials or personal payloads.
data.unknown: No marketing message was sent, profile was changed or account limit was exercised. The public guide does not establish a universal quota for every endpoint, and this article does not infer one. Account-specific limits, exact retry timing and revision-specific payload changes need the corresponding endpoint reference. Examples describe a client design and test strategy, not a measured production workload.
data.author: Reverse Engineer Lab
data.models: Illustrative scheduling example: a worker sends many requests at the start of each minute, then remains idle. Its average can look acceptable while the first second exceeds a burst allowance. Smoothing dispatch changes the burst profile; it does not increase the published account allowance. The example intentionally uses no hard-coded Klaviyo quota because tiers vary by operation.
data.workflows:
A useful client record includes the endpoint, selected revision, operation identity and outcome category. On a capacity response, honor the documented retry guidance and coordinate workers sharing that account. On a revision upgrade, replay a small set of representative, authorized test requests and compare response shapes before expanding traffic.

A focused compatibility check should inspect fields that the application actually uses, not only whether a request returns 200. A successful response with a changed optional field can still alter downstream behavior. Preserve the old and new expected shapes as test fixtures with all customer data removed.

data.title: WooCommerce: Store API versus order storage
data.target_version: WooCommerce 11.2.1 research baseline; Store API v1 documentation
data.question: Which layer should an integration inspect when a store changes order storage? WooCommerce exposes a customer-facing Store API while HPOS changes persistence behind the order model. This investigation separates public shopping operations, merchant data access and storage selection.
data.summary: Why a customer-facing API, merchant order access and HPOS are different layers—and why table existence alone cannot identify authoritative orders.
data.observed:
The Store API is documented for customer-facing products, carts and checkout. It is distinct from merchant-oriented WooCommerce REST access and does not expose arbitrary sensitive store or customer data. Public-facing does not mean every operation is an unrestricted read: cart and checkout behavior has its own documented context and protections.

HPOS stores order data in purpose-built tables through WooCommerce’s CRUD model. The documentation covers compatibility and synchronization with the legacy storage arrangement. The selected authoritative storage mode matters; the existence of custom order tables alone is not a complete statement about which data a store currently uses.
data.inferred:
The stable integration boundary is the supported order abstraction, not a guessed table name. Reading a table directly can accidentally select a synchronized copy, an inactive storage path or an incomplete extension view. An API or CRUD operation can preserve the application’s selected storage behavior, although extension compatibility still needs verification.

This also explains why storefront and back-office checks should not be combined. A working product/cart endpoint proves one customer-facing path. It does not prove that a merchant export reads all orders from the authoritative datastore.
data.unknown: No merchant database, customer record, payment credential or proprietary plugin data is published here. The analysis does not assert that every extension supports HPOS or that synchronized tables are always current. It also does not establish checkout race behavior. Version-specific core and extension contracts should be checked before a storage migration; the cited source baseline is the one identified in the entry metadata.
data.author: Reverse Engineer Lab
data.models: Conceptual model: customer storefront → Store API; merchant integration → authorized order interface; order interface → selected datastore. HPOS belongs at the persistence boundary. A storefront request does not select the datastore merely by using a particular REST namespace.
data.workflows:
Illustrative migration check: a store has both legacy and custom order tables after an upgrade. An investigator should first determine the configured authoritative mode and compatibility status, then compare a known order through the supported order interface before judging raw table counts. Zero rows in one table are not sufficient evidence that the store has no orders.

A useful test set includes a recent order, an older order, a refund and an order containing extension data. Verify the operations the integration needs against the selected storage mode. Keep any real customer data out of published fixtures. This article proposes that test boundary without reproducing a merchant migration.

data.title: Notion: databases, data sources and pages
data.question: Why does a database ID no longer identify every table-shaped operation in Notion? The 2025-09-03 API model separates the visible database container from its data sources. This investigation follows the consequences for an integration that previously assumed one database meant one schema.
data.summary: The practical consequences of Notion’s database/data-source split for schema discovery, page creation and integration identity.
data.observed:
Notion’s upgrade guide introduces the separation between database containers and data sources. A database can contain multiple data sources. A data source owns its property schema, and pages are records under that source whose property values must conform to the schema. The reference offers separate operations for retrieving and querying a data source.

This is an API-model distinction, not simply a display rename. Container identity, table/schema identity and page identity now answer different questions. A request written around the older one-to-one assumption needs an explicit source-selection step when more than one source is possible.
data.inferred:
A client should not silently choose the first source returned by a container and assume it represents the user’s intended table. Persist the selected data-source ID with the integration’s mapping. If that source becomes unavailable or changes, surface the mismatch instead of writing into a different source that happens to be visible.

Property names are another layer of identity. A user-facing label can change while the application still needs to understand which property its mapping refers to. Schema discovery and validation should be explicit parts of an upgrade rather than incidental consequences of the first write.
data.unknown: The article addresses the cited 2025-09-03 model change rather than every later Notion API feature. It does not reproduce workspace permissions, concurrent schema edits or a multi-source migration. No private workspace content or undocumented client protocol is included. Verify the actual API revision and the chosen source’s schema before applying the model to a live integration.
data.author: Reverse Engineer Lab
data.models: Conceptual model: database container → one or more data sources → pages. The container organizes sources; each source supplies a schema; each page supplies values for that schema. An integration configuration should identify the layer it stores instead of calling all three objects “database.”
data.workflows:
Illustrative scenario: an integration used to store a database ID for a task table. After the model change, the containing database offers Tasks and Milestones as separate sources. The client must identify the intended source, retrieve its schema and validate its field mapping before it queries or creates pages. Choosing whichever source appears first could produce valid requests against the wrong table.

A bounded upgrade test would retrieve the container, enumerate accessible sources, select one explicitly, read its schema, and query a small known set of pages. Check behavior when the configured source is missing or access is removed. This is a proposed test, not an operation performed on a user workspace.
